sections.overview: The tawny owl is a stocky, resident woodland owl of much of Europe and parts of Asia and North Africa. It hunts mainly at night, often from a perch, and stays close to a familiar territory through the year. A rounded head without ear tufts, dark eyes and richly patterned brown or grey plumage make it recognizable even when its bark-like colours conceal it against a tree. The North African form mauritanica, sometimes separated as the Maghreb owl, is included within Strix aluco by the 2025 Clements checklist.
sections.identification: In BTO ringing samples, adult females averaged 502 g and a 274 mm wing, while males averaged 396 g and a 259 mm wing. A general reference gives 37–46 cm body length and 81–104 cm wingspan; no reliable body-width measure was found. Adults have a rounded head, a plain facial disc, a short hooked bill and no raised ear tufts. The eyes are dark brown to nearly black and face forward. Across Europe, plumage ranges from chestnut red-brown through grey-brown to paler grey; these are colour forms within the species, not separate sexes. Males and females look alike, although females are larger on average and the size ranges overlap. Fine streaks and mottling break up the outline against bark. The broad, rounded wings and compact body suit manoeuvring among trees.
sections.habitat: Broad-leaved and mixed woodland provide mature trees, sheltered roosts and cavities for nesting. Tawny owls also occupy conifer plantations, wooded parks and large gardens, provided that trees or nest boxes offer a suitable cavity and nearby ground supplies prey. They avoid extensive open country and uplands without tree cover. Adults remain on established territories year-round; young birds usually disperse only a few kilometres, and large stretches of water can impede their spread. Habitat quality therefore depends on both nesting sites and connected, huntable cover.
sections.diet: Small mammals, especially mice and voles, are common prey, but the owl takes whatever suitable animals are available: small birds, amphibians, large insects and earthworms. On damp nights it may catch worms on lawns; observations also include bats near roosts. Pellet studies show why a single menu cannot describe every pair: prey remains vary with season, habitat and local animal abundance, and the owls can switch to other prey when rodents are scarce. Fur, feathers and bones that cannot be digested are regurgitated as compact pellets, which let researchers reconstruct local feeding patterns.
sections.behavior: This is a mainly nocturnal hunter that often waits on a perch, watches for movement, then glides down to seize prey with its feet. Its broad facial disc helps collect sound, while forward-facing eyes provide overlapping vision for judging distance. Tawny owls can locate prey by listening as well as looking. Their flight is very quiet, though not literally soundless: experiments on tawny owl wings found that removing leading-edge feather serrations increased noise shortly before landing, showing that the effect depends on flight phase. A male’s territorial hoot and a female’s sharper “keewik” may overlap as a pair duet. The familiar “twit-twoo” is therefore often two birds’ calls, not one individual producing a single phrase.
sections.reproduction: Pairs nest in tree cavities or nest boxes and may lay their first eggs as early as February in Britain, although many begin in March or later. Incubation starts with the first egg, so chicks hatch at different times; when food is limited, this can allow at least some of the brood to survive. Young leave the nest while still unable to fly. During this “branching” stage they climb, hop and flutter around nearby branches, calling to adults, which continue to find and feed them outside the cavity. Leaving the nest is thus a normal developmental step, not proof that a chick has been abandoned.
sections.ecology: By feeding on small mammals and changing prey when their numbers fluctuate, tawny owls link woodland food webs to local prey communities. Pellet contents offer a practical record of that relationship: a two-territory study in Ukraine found seasonal, annual and habitat variation in mammal remains, with alternative prey represented as well as rodents. The owl’s dependence on cavities also ties its breeding distribution to the supply of old trees and nest boxes. Because established pairs defend territories through the year, suitable nesting cavities and hunting ground must occur within the same local landscape.
sections.conservation: BirdLife International’s global owl-species account consulted on 11 October 2026 lists the tawny owl as Least Concern. That global category does not mean every national population is secure: in Britain, the British Trust for Ornithology reports that the species has been Amber-listed since 2015 because of concern about long-term decline. British monitoring remains incomplete because a nocturnal bird is difficult to survey, and the BTO identifies population change, breeding success and survival as continuing knowledge gaps. Availability of nest cavities and prey also shapes local suitability, so national concern and global category describe different geographic scales.
